new_steps.note: から and ので gave reasons. Stage 9 gave blame and credit. These patterns give reasons a REGISTER: the shop-notice reason, the just-like-them reason, the all-the-more reason. Reading them is reading between lines.

points.en: from the fact that — the evidence reason

exp.what: A reason presented as evidence: 窓が開いていることから、誰かが入ったと分かる — from the open window, we can tell someone came in. Where から states a cause, ことから presents an observed fact and draws the conclusion in public. It is also the set pattern for naming origins: 形が富士山に似ていることから、この名前がついた.
exp.build: Plain clause + ことから: 人気があることから, 音がしないことから. The following clause is typically a conclusion, discovery or naming.
exp.when: Explanations, guidebooks, quiz shows — anywhere a fact is being reasoned FROM rather than merely blamed. The naming use is everywhere in place-name lore.
exp.watch: The reason must be observable. A feeling reasons with から; ことから wants something you could point at.

ex: 行列ができていることから、あの店の人気が分かる。
You can tell how popular that shop is from the queue outside.
雪が多いことから、この地方は「雪国」と呼ばれる。
From its heavy snow, this region is called 'snow country'.

exp.what: A reason built on character: 真面目な彼のことだから、時間通りに来るだろう — knowing how conscientious he is, he'll be on time. The pattern only works on people (and person-like things) whose habits both speakers know, and it always launches a prediction.
exp.build: Person + の + ことだから + a prediction: 田中さんのことだから、もう終わっているよ. The person usually carries a describing clause that names the trait doing the predicting.
exp.when: Reassuring someone, excusing someone, betting on someone — social reasoning among people who share context. It is warm grammar; it says 'we both know them.'
exp.watch: It needs the shared knowledge. About a stranger it fails socially rather than grammatically — the listener hears an intimacy that doesn't exist.

ex: 彼のことだから、締め切りは必ず守るだろう。
Knowing him, he'll meet the deadline without fail.
心配性の母のことだから、もう駅に着いているはずだ。
Knowing my worrier of a mother, she's already at the station.

exp.what: A reason with a lever in it: 期待していただけに、がっかりした — precisely BECAUSE I had hoped, the disappointment was bigger. だけに takes a background fact and uses it to amplify the reaction, in either direction: bigger letdown, bigger joy.
exp.build: Plain clause／noun + だけに: 有名なだけに, 練習しただけに. The second clause carries a feeling or evaluation scaled UP by the first.
exp.when: Reactions with history behind them: results after long effort, prices at famous shops, upsets after favourites. Sports commentary runs on it.
exp.watch: The second half must scale with the first. A flat consequence (雨だっただけに、傘をさした) wastes the lever — から was enough there.

ex: 評判の店だけに、味は期待以上だった。
Given its reputation, the food exceeded even expectation.
練習してきただけに、負けて悔しい。
All that practice — which is exactly why losing stings.

exp.what: だけに's satisfied sibling: 専門家だけあって、説明が分かりやすい — being an expert, sure enough, the explanations are clear. The observed quality MATCHES the credential, and the speaker is nodding along. Admiration is built into the grammar.
exp.build: Plain clause／noun + だけあって: 高いだけあって, 十年住んだだけあって. Often paired with さすがに in the same breath.
exp.when: Compliments with reasons attached — hotels worth their price, veterans worth their years. The set where expectations are met, never dashed.
exp.watch: This is the fork from だけに: だけあって only goes to fulfilled expectations. Disappointment must switch back to だけに — 高いだけあってまずい contradicts itself.

ex: さすが経験者だけあって、仕事が早い。
As you'd expect from someone experienced, the work is fast.
有名なホテルだけあって、サービスが素晴らしい。
It lives up to its name — the hotel's service is superb.

exp.what: The notice-board reason: 工事中につき、通行止め — due to construction, road closed. Four words, no verb, a bow implied. につき is how institutions give reasons: cold, brief, and pasted to a door.
exp.build: Noun + につき + the consequence, often verbless: 本日休業日につき, 雨天につき中止. (A second, unrelated meaning — per unit: 一人につき二枚 — reads from context.)
exp.when: READING, overwhelmingly: shutters, gates, elevators, event notices. Producing it belongs to whoever writes the notice — which one day is you, drafting the office sign.
exp.watch: It is paper grammar. Said aloud in conversation it sounds like reading a sign — ので owns the spoken register.

ex: 店内改装につき、しばらく休業いたします。
Due to renovation, we will be closed for a while.
強風につき、本日の運転は中止します。
Due to strong winds, today's service is cancelled.

exp.what: A reason that binds: 引き受けた以上、最後までやる — having taken it on, I see it through. 以上 turns a done fact into an obligation on the speaker: the die is cast, so the conduct follows.
exp.build: Plain clause + 以上（は）+ resolve/obligation/advice: 約束した以上, 学生である以上. The second half wants べきだ, なければならない, つもりだ — the duty shapes.
exp.when: Statements of principle and spine: contracts entered, roles accepted, countries moved to. 日本に住む以上、日本語を勉強するべきだ is the learner's own sentence.
exp.watch: The first clause must be settled and chosen. 雨が降る以上 misfires — weather commits nobody. からには is its near-twin and swaps in freely.

ex: 契約した以上、支払いの義務がある。
Having signed the contract, you are obliged to pay.
やると言った以上、途中でやめるわけにはいかない。
Having said I'd do it, backing out midway isn't an option.

points.en: the grammar taped to the door

exp.what: Japan communicates institutionally through short pasted notices, and they share one dialect: につき for the reason, ご迷惑をおかけします for the apology, ご了承ください for the closing bow. 本日休業日につき — four words carrying a full sentence of regret.
exp.build: The skeleton of nearly every notice: [reason]につき、[consequence]。ご迷惑をおかけしますが、ご了承ください。 Learn it once and a wall of paper becomes one form letter.
exp.when: Shutters, station gates, elevator doors, clinic windows. The reading payoff is immediate and daily — this register is met more often than any spoken keigo.
exp.watch: The apology lines are formulae, not feelings — ご迷惑をおかけします measures the notice's politeness, not the inconvenience's size. Reading emotional weight into stock phrases is the reverse of the mistake of missing it in real ones.

ex: 点検につき、エレベーターは使えません。ご了承ください。
Due to inspection, the elevator is out of use. We appreciate your understanding.

exp.what: Write a three-line notice: reason (につき), consequence, apology formula. Then rewrite the same fact as one SPOKEN line to a friend (ので).
exp.build: The pair is the exercise: 雨天につき、中止します／雨だから、中止だって。 Same fact, two registers, no overlap in vocabulary.
exp.when: Register-switching on one fact is the core N2 writing skill — this drills it on the smallest possible canvas.
exp.watch: If your notice contains です・ます AND につき but also から, the registers have bled. Notices are all-formal or they are not notices.

ex: 社内清掃につき、午後は入れません。
Due to office cleaning, no entry this afternoon.

new_steps.note: Stage 9's Step 31 drew conclusions; Step 39 denied inferences. This step is certainty's top shelf — the four ways to stake your name on a claim, and the one pattern for saying it merely looks that way.

exp.what: An identification sealed shut: 成功は努力の結果にほかならない — the success is nothing other than the result of effort. The pattern doesn't just assert; it excludes every alternative in the same breath.
exp.build: Noun + にほかならない: 誤解にほかならない, 愛情にほかならない. Essay Japanese; the noun is usually an interpretation or essence, not a physical object.
exp.when: The thesis sentence of an argument — the moment a writer stops weighing and names the thing. One per essay is about the right dose.
exp.watch: It identifies; it doesn't predict. Future events can't wear it — 明日は雨にほかならない is broken. For predictions, the next pattern.

ex: この結果は、毎日の練習の成果にほかならない。
This result is nothing other than the fruit of daily practice.
それは誤解にほかなりません。
That is nothing but a misunderstanding.

exp.what: に違いない from Stage 9, promoted to writing: same 'must be,' harder collar. 犯人はあの男に相違ない reads like a detective's report because that is the register it lives in — findings, testimony, formal conclusions.
exp.build: Noun／plain clause + に相違ない: 本物に相違ない, 彼が書いたに相違ない. Documents also use 相違ありません as the sworn-statement form — 記載内容に相違ありません, the contents are correct as written.
exp.when: Written conclusions and official confirmations. The 相違ありません form is one you will SIGN — it sits above the line on applications confirming everything is true.
exp.watch: In conversation it costumes you as a detective; に違いない remains the spoken form. The two are a register pair, not a nuance pair.

ex: この証言から見て、彼が犯人に相違ない。
From this testimony, he is without doubt the culprit.
上記の内容に相違ありません。
The above contents are correct (as written) — the application formula.

exp.what: The spoken shelf's top: そんなの、うそに決まっている — that's obviously a lie. Grammatical certainty plus emotional pressure; the speaker isn't concluding, they're refusing to entertain the alternative.
exp.build: Plain form／noun + に決まっている: 無理に決まっている, 勝つに決まっている. Casual speech shortens the orbit: 〜に決まってるじゃん.
exp.when: Conversation, argument, reassurance (大丈夫に決まっている). This is where the certainty family finally gets to be loud.
exp.watch: The heat is the point and the risk: at a superior it reads as talking back. The exam distinction — はずだ reasons, に違いない infers, に決まっている insists.

ex: そんなうまい話、うそに決まっているよ。
A deal that good is obviously a lie.
彼が謝るべきに決まっている。
Obviously HE'S the one who should apologise.

exp.what: A verdict appealing to common sense: それは無理というものだ — that, you see, is asking too much. The speaker holds the claim up as something everyone would recognise: this is what fairness/rudeness/asking-too-much looks like.
exp.build: Plain clause／noun + というものだ: 当たり前というものだ, 親心というものだ. The negative というものではない softens a general claim: 高ければいいというものではない — expensive doesn't simply mean good.
exp.when: Gentle verdicts and proverbs-on-the-spot; the negative form is the essay workhorse for pushing back on simple equations.
exp.watch: No past tense, no personal subject — the pattern speaks for common sense, and common sense has no yesterday. 私は嬉しいというものだ misfires; it was never about you.

ex: 初対面でそれを聞くのは、失礼というものだ。
Asking that on first meeting — that's what rudeness is.
安ければいいというものではない。
Cheap isn't automatically good.

exp.what: The counterweight to the whole step: everything else here commits, かのようだ steps back into open pretence. まるで夢であるかのようだ — as if it were a dream, and both of us know it isn't. Stage 10's まるで〜ようだ compared appearances; かのようだ marks the appearance as contrary to fact.
exp.build: Plain clause + かのようだ／かのように＋verb／かのような＋noun: 何も知らないかのように話す. まるで loves to open the sentence.
exp.when: Written description with literary temperature — snow like a stage set, a silence as if time had stopped. It is the novelist's たとえ.
exp.watch: The claim must be FALSE and both parties aware: 彼は病気であるかのようだ about someone actually sick collapses into slander of the truth. Real resemblance keeps plain ようだ.

ex: 彼は何も聞いていないかのように、仕事を続けた。
He kept working as if he'd heard nothing.
町は、時間が止まったかのように静かだった。
The town was quiet, as if time had stopped.

points.jp: 確信のはしご・二段目

exp.what: The ladder now runs floor to ceiling, and register splits it in two. Spoken, climbing: かもしれない → だろう → はずだ → に違いない → に決まっている. Written, climbing: 〜と思われる → はずである → に相違ない → にほかならない. Same heights, different buildings.
exp.build: Choose the rung by evidence, the building by medium. A hunch in a report is と思われる; a certainty in a kitchen is に決まってる. The sworn form 相違ありません stands slightly apart — it certifies rather than argues.
exp.when: Every opinion you voice picks a rung whether you choose it or not. This builder is for choosing.
exp.watch: The classic overreach is importing certainty DOWN the register: に決まっている in an essay reads as shouting; にほかならない over dinner reads as a lecture. Height and building are independent choices.

ex: 彼は来ないに決まっている。／彼は来ないと思われる。
He's obviously not coming. / It would appear he is not coming. (same claim, two buildings)

exp.what: A four-line detective's note: the observed fact (ことから), the deduction (に相違ない), the alternative dismissed (わけがない, from Stage 10), and the verdict (にほかならない).
exp.build: Shape to steal: 窓が開いていることから、犯人は外から入ったに相違ない。中からのはずがない。これは計画的な犯行にほかならない。
exp.when: The certainty patterns only settle when forced to work together — a deduction chain is the smallest structure that forces them.
exp.watch: One claim per rung. If two sentences share a certainty level, the chain isn't climbing.

ex: 足あとがないことから、犯人はまだ中にいるに相違ない。
From the absence of footprints, the culprit must still be inside.

new_steps.note: The stage closes where N2 lives: the written register. Documents, reports, applications — the Japanese that is typed, stamped and filed. Every pattern here has a spoken equivalent the learner already owns; the lesson is the costume change.

exp.what: で and に put things places; における does the same job wearing a tie: 日本における教育, education in Japan — as a report would title it. It marks the arena of a topic rather than the location of an action.
exp.build: Noun + における + noun: 会議における発言, 現代における役割. Sentence-medial: においては. Strictly noun-connecting — verbs keep で.
exp.when: Titles, headings, theses, slides. If the sentence could be a section heading, における belongs; if it could be said across a table, it doesn't.
exp.watch: The classic overuse is spoken: 学校における友達 in conversation is a costume at a picnic. で survives every spoken need.

ex: 日本における人口の減少が、大きな問題になっている。
Population decline in Japan has become a major problem.
会議における彼の発言が、話題になった。
His remarks at the meeting became the talk of the office.

exp.what: Two readings off one shape, split by the verb form in front. After た-form: proper sequence — よく考えた上で決めた, decided upon due consideration; the first step was the qualified basis for the second. After dictionary form: in the course of / for the purpose of — 申請する上で必要な書類, documents necessary in applying.
exp.build: た-form + 上で for the sequence; dictionary form + 上で for the in-doing. The nominal version 〜の上で works for both: 相談の上で.
exp.when: Procedures and prefaces: contracts want 確認の上、ご署名ください; guides want 生活する上での注意. It is てから with the casualness drained out and deliberation poured in.
exp.watch: The two readings do not mix: 考える上で決めた is neither. Check the verb form first — it is the whole meaning.

ex: 内容をよく確認した上で、サインしてください。
Please sign after — and on the basis of — checking the contents carefully.
日本で働く上で、敬語は避けて通れない。
In working in Japan, keigo is unavoidable.

exp.what: Stage 10's につれて tracked one change dragging another. に伴って is its document-grade twin, and it also covers events with attendants: 引っ越しに伴って住所が変わった — with the move came the address change. Change A, and B in its train.
exp.build: Noun／dictionary-form verb + に伴って／に伴い (the い-form is the more written): 高齢化に伴い, 制度の変更に伴って.
exp.when: Reports of linked change: populations, prices, systems. The pattern of every news paragraph beginning 'with the increase in…'
exp.watch: Both sides must move or happen — a static pairing (机に伴って椅子がある) has nothing accompanying anything. And in conversation, と一緒に or につれて still do the living-room version.

ex: インターネットの普及に伴って、生活が大きく変わった。
With the spread of the internet, life changed profoundly.
転勤に伴い、来月引っ越します。
In connection with my transfer, I move next month.

exp.what: 前に with a programme printed: 開会に先立って、黙とうが行われた — prior to the opening, a silence was observed. 先立つ is 'to go ahead of'; the pattern schedules a lesser formal act before a greater one.
exp.build: Noun／dictionary-form verb + に先立って／に先立ち: 発表に先立ち, 工事に先立って. The thing before に先立って is the MAIN event; the clause is the preliminary.
exp.when: Ceremonies, launches, official processes — the register where events have preliminaries at all. Speeches and news reports own it.
exp.watch: Both events need formality and connection: 昼ご飯に先立って手を洗った is a comedy of scale. 前に remains the everyday word — this is its dress uniform.

ex: 新製品の発売に先立って、発表会が開かれた。
Prior to the product's release, a launch event was held.
面接に先立ち、書類審査が行われます。
Prior to interviews, documents will be screened.

exp.what: An event turned into a hinge: 結婚を機に、引っ越した — taking the marriage as the occasion, we moved. The named event isn't the cause so much as the chosen turning point; the speaker made it one.
exp.build: Noun／dictionary-form verb + の + を機に: 卒業を機に, 病気を機に. The heavier をきっかけに swaps in with a nuance of chance rather than choice.
exp.when: Life-change narration — the self-introduction's load-bearing pattern. Résumés, first conversations, and the sentence about why you came to Japan.
exp.watch: The event should be a milestone. 昼休みを機に転職した reads as satire; the pattern spends significance, and small occasions can't cover the bill.

ex: 転職を機に、東京から引っ越しました。
I took the job change as the occasion to move away from Tokyo.
入院を機に、生活を見直した。
The hospital stay became my occasion to rethink how I live.

exp.what: One classical stem, two modern jobs. つつ（も）is written concession-or-parallel: 悪いと知りつつ（も）— while knowing it was wrong. つつある is ongoing change caught mid-motion: 回復しつつある — in the process of recovering. Both are ながら's literary relatives.
exp.build: Verb ます-stem + つつ／つつも／つつある: 思いつつ, 増えつつある. The FORMS table on verb cards carries つつ from this point on.
exp.when: つつも for written self-aware contradiction (knowing better, doing anyway); つつある for reports of trends in motion — economies, recoveries, declines. Neither belongs in casual speech.
exp.watch: つつある differs from ている exactly where it matters: 変わっている is a state already reached, 変わりつつある is the changing itself. Trend sentences almost always want the second.

ex: 体に悪いと知りつつも、夜ふかしを続けている。
While knowing it's bad for me, I keep staying up late.
この町の人口は、減少しつつある。
This town's population is in the process of declining.

exp.what: けど climbed all the rungs: が, のに, くせに — and ものの is the written landing: 申し込んだものの、行けるかどうか分からない — I applied, though whether I can go is another matter. Concession without のに's frustration or くせに's accusation: just the fact, then the complication.
exp.build: Plain form + ものの: 買ったものの, 便利なものの (na-adjectives take な／である). The second clause often trails into uncertainty — 〜かどうか分からない is its favourite ending.
exp.when: Written reflection and reports: things done whose outcomes wobble. The pattern of half-finished plans and honest progress reports.
exp.watch: ものの stays cool — it cannot carry のに's sting. 約束したのに来なかった accuses; 約束したものの来られなかった merely records. Choosing between them IS the register choice.

ex: 申請書を出したものの、承認されるかどうか分からない。
I submitted the application, though whether it will be approved is another question.
日本語を三年勉強したものの、敬語はまだ難しい。
Though I've studied Japanese three years, keigo is still hard.

points.jp: 書きことばという別の国
points.en: written Japanese is a second country

exp.what: Formal written Japanese is not polite spoken Japanese written down — it is a parallel register with its own vocabulary table. だ・である replaces です・ます in reports; 〜より (from) opens official mail; 及び means and, 並びに means and-between-groups; する verbs shed する in headlines (来月値上げ). The patterns of this stage — における, に伴い, に先立ち — are its native grammar.
exp.build: The conversion table worth owning early: でも→しかし, だから→したがって, どんどん→急速に, とても→非常に. One column is your speech; the other is every document you will file.
exp.when: Reading official mail, writing anything an office will stamp, and — the quiet payoff — recognising why NHK subtitles and LINE messages feel like different languages. They are.
exp.watch: The registers must not leak INTO each other: したがって in chat is as wrong as だから in a report. N2's writing section is largely a test of keeping the two countries' borders.

ex: 会議の資料は、木曜までに提出のこと。
Meeting materials to be submitted by Thursday. (the noticeboard imperative — のこと)

exp.what: Write one application paragraph in である-register: the occasion (を機に), the basis (上で), the concession (ものの), and the request. Then say the same thing to a friend in three casual lines.
exp.build: Shape to steal: 転職を機に、貴校での学習を希望する。仕事を続けつつの通学になるものの、検討した上での決断である。
exp.when: This is the N2 writing task in miniature, and the two-register rewrite is the whole skill this stage taught.
exp.watch: The casual rewrite is not a decoration — if you cannot say it plainly, the formal version was probably assembled rather than meant.

ex: よく考えた上での決断であるものの、不安もある。
It is a decision made upon due consideration — though not without anxiety.

exp.what: Thirty-seven doors into N2's first rooms: refusal with a collar on, occasions and their speeches, scope declared edge to edge, reasons with registers, certainty at full height, and the written country. If Stage 9 taught arguing and Stage 10 taught precision, this stage taught FORMALITY as a working tool rather than a costume.
exp.build: The quiz draws across all six steps. The pairs that share a doorway are the ones worth re-checking: ざるを得ない／ようがない, に際して／にあたって, のみならず／はもとより, だけに／だけあって, に違いない／に相違ない, つつ／ながら, ものの／のに.
exp.when: Before moving on — Stage 12 assumes every register here is load-bearing.
exp.watch: The stage's single most common error family is register bleed: a spoken certainty in a written sentence, a notice-reason said aloud. When in doubt, ask WHERE the sentence lives before asking what it means.

ex: 以上の理由につき、本申請を承認せざるを得ない。
For the above reasons, this application cannot but be approved. (five patterns, one sentence — the stage in miniature)
